- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots; cap forecast at +3% above prior peak or use 20-day moving average as ceiling.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.4) and price is trending up, model frequently overcorrects; apply downward bias of 0.5–1.5% to avoid overbought bias.
- When sentiment is volatile or oscillating (e.g., alternating 0.1–0.5), model exhibits lag; shift forecast 1–2 days backward in trend if price is trending down.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture mean reversion; if 18-day average is >10% above recent 30-day mean, reduce forecast by 2–4% to align with reversion bias.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.1) and price is falling, model often underestimates; add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to avoid “panic” underestimation.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model tends to overestimate; apply downward adjustment of 1–2% to avoid “bullish trap” bias.
